question: What are the three main functions of the nervous system?

options.C: Sensory input, integration, and motor output

explanation: The nervous system works by first detecting changes, processing that information, and then sending commands to the body. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h1)

question: An effector organ in the nervous system refers to which structures?
explanation: Effectors are the organs that carry out the final motor response dictated by the central nervous system. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h1)

question: The two main cell types found in nervous tissue are neurons and...
explanation: Nervous tissue is built from impulse-transmitting neurons and supporting glial cells. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h2)

question: Why do mature neurons struggle to heal or replace themselves after severe injury?

options.A: They do not contain any genetic material or DNA
options.B: They are constantly destroyed by neuroglial cells
options.C: They lose their ability to divide during development
options.D: They lack a cell membrane to protect their interior

explanation: Most mature neurons exit the cell cycle permanently, meaning lost neurons are extremely difficult for the body to replace. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h2)

question: Which part of a neuron typically receives incoming signals from other cells?
explanation: Dendrites act as receiving antennae, picking up chemical and electrical signals from neighboring neurons. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h3)

question: A neuron with one axon and multiple dendrites extending from its cell body is classified as...
explanation: Multipolar neurons have three or more processes and make up the vast majority of neurons in the brain and spinal cord. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h3)

question: Which glial cell forms the insulating myelin sheath in the central nervous system?
explanation: Oligodendrocytes wrap their flat extensions around multiple central nervous system axons to create myelin. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h4)

question: A patient develops an infection in the central nervous system. Which glial cell will primarily act as a phagocyte to clear away debris?
explanation: Microglia transform into active macrophages to clear out damaged tissue and foreign invaders in the brain and spinal cord. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h4)

question: What is the primary purpose of the myelin sheath on a nerve fiber?

options.A: To increase the speed of nerve impulse conduction
options.B: To anchor the neuron firmly to surrounding bone tissue
options.C: To generate new chemical neurotransmitters for the synapse
options.D: To supply the axon with oxygen and glucose nutrients

explanation: Myelin acts as an electrical insulator, allowing signals to travel much faster down the axon. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h5)

question: The microscopic gaps found between adjacent Schwann cells along a myelinated axon are called...
explanation: Nodes of Ranvier expose the axonal membrane to the extracellular fluid, enabling saltatory conduction. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h5)

question: During the depolarization phase of an action potential, which ion rushes into the neuron?
explanation: The opening of voltage-gated sodium channels allows positive sodium ions to flood into the cell interior. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h6)

question: What does a resting membrane potential of -70 millivolts indicate about the inside of the neuron?

options.A: It contains equal amounts of positive and negative ions
options.B: It is more positively charged than the extracellular fluid
options.C: It is completely devoid of any electrical charge
options.D: It is more negatively charged than the outside

explanation: The negative sign signifies that the intracellular environment has an excess of negative charge relative to the outside. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h6)

question: Which ion influx at the axon terminal triggers the release of neurotransmitter vesicles?
explanation: Calcium entry into the axon terminal is the direct trigger that causes synaptic vesicles to release their chemical cargo. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h7)

question: What is the precise role of neurotransmitters in neural communication?

options.A: To carry chemical signals across the synaptic cleft between cells
options.B: To physically connect the axon of one neuron to another's dendrite
options.C: To provide metabolic energy directly to the post-synaptic neuron
options.D: To permanently insulate the electrical pathways of the brain

explanation: Because electrical currents cannot jump the physical gap of the synapse, neurotransmitters act as chemical bridges. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h7)

question: Which part of the nervous system has a much better capacity for tissue regeneration?
explanation: Peripheral nerves can regenerate with the help of Schwann cells, whereas the central nervous system discourages axon regrowth. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h8)

question: What is the primary function of the regeneration tube formed by Schwann cells in injured peripheral nerves?

options.A: To supply red blood cells for systemic oxygen transport
options.B: To guide the growing axon tip back to its target
options.C: To dissolve scar tissue forming around the injury site
options.D: To manufacture new neurotransmitters for the brain

explanation: Schwann cells proliferate and align to form a hollow tube that directs the regenerating axonal sprout forward. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h8)
